notes: Consumer GPUs are ranked here for local-LLM practicality rather than gaming performance. VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, runtime support, board power, acquisition cost and physical integration matter more than gaming FPS.
Prices are point-in-time Canadian observations. Retailer stock and pricing can change quickly.
Vendor AI TOPS figures are datatype- and implementation-dependent and are not directly comparable across Intel, NVIDIA and AMD.
Model-size guidance is approximate and assumes quantized inference with additional headroom required for KV cache, context and runtime overhead.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: Strongest with runtimes that explicitly support Intel GPU/XMX paths; Vulkan offers a broader fallback. GGUF compatibility depends on the selected inference engine rather than the GPU alone.
hardware.model_size_practicality: Best suited to roughly 7B-class models at higher-quality quantization and some 12B-14B-class models at tighter quantization/context settings. 12GB VRAM is the principal capacity limit.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Excellent acquisition-cost-to-bandwidth ratio for a new actively cooled card, but less mature and less universally supported than CUDA.
hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 456 GB/s at 190W is approximately 2.40 GB/s of memory bandwidth per watt using reference TBP; this is only a coarse hardware ratio, not measured LLM efficiency.
hardware.off_grid_notes: 190W reference board power is manageable compared with high-end GPUs, but whole-system draw still requires substantially more energy than embedded or 70W workstation cards.

pricing.note: Sparkle B580 12GB clearance listing; an open-box unit was also listed for less.

hardware.power_connector_reference: 1x PCIe 8-pin or PCIe Gen 5 cable; partner cards vary
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Broad support for common CUDA-backed FP16/BF16, INT8/INT4 and GGUF quantized inference paths; exact kernel support depends on runtime/version.
hardware.model_size_practicality: 16GB VRAM is comfortable for many 7B-14B quantized models and can fit some larger models only with aggressive quantization/offload. Context and KV cache can materially reduce usable weight capacity.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Strong general-purpose local-LLM choice when CUDA compatibility is valued more than maximum VRAM-per-dollar.
hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 448 GB/s at 180W is approximately 2.49 GB/s of memory bandwidth per watt using reference TGP; actual inference efficiency depends strongly on clocks, kernels and quantization.
hardware.off_grid_notes: 180W reference TGP is workable for a solar-backed desktop but far above dedicated low-power inference accelerators; idle and whole-system measurements should be captured separately.

pricing.note: MSI 16GB listing observed at CA$829.99; partner-card prices vary.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: GGUF/Vulkan paths are broadly practical; ROCm/HIP acceleration depends on the installed ROCm and runtime support matrix for this consumer RDNA 4 GPU.
hardware.model_size_practicality: 16GB VRAM targets many 7B-14B quantized models well. Larger models generally require tighter quantization and/or CPU/system-memory offload.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: Compelling for inexpensive 16GB local inference when Vulkan/ROCm compatibility has been verified for the intended stack; lower bandwidth than RX 9070 but lower power and purchase cost.
hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 320 GB/s at 160W is 2.00 GB/s of memory bandwidth per watt using AMD reference TBP.
hardware.off_grid_notes: 160W TBP is relatively restrained for a 16GB desktop GPU, making it one of the more plausible consumer cards for power-constrained systems if software compatibility is acceptable.

pricing.note: Sapphire Pulse RX 9060 XT 16GB listing observed at CA$649.99 sale price; other partner variants differed.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: 16GB capacity is the limiting factor; Vulkan/GGUF paths can be practical while ROCm/HIP support should be checked against the exact runtime version.
hardware.model_size_practicality: Similar capacity class to RTX 5060 Ti 16GB and RX 9060 XT 16GB, but 640 GB/s bandwidth makes it substantially more attractive for memory-bandwidth-bound decode when the model fits entirely or mostly in VRAM.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: One of the strongest current consumer 16GB candidates on raw memory bandwidth and reasonable 220W TBP, provided the target inference stack supports RDNA 4 well.
hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 640 GB/s at 220W is approximately 2.91 GB/s of memory bandwidth per watt using AMD reference TBP.
hardware.off_grid_notes: 220W is materially higher than RX 9060 XT but still below many high-end workstation/consumer GPUs; the doubled bandwidth can justify the additional power for bandwidth-bound inference.

pricing.note: Acer Nitro RX 9070 OC 16GB clearance listing observed at CA$899.88.
